question: What promises does the LORD make to Joshua right after the death of Moses?
What link does the text make between being “courageous” and meditating on the Book of the Law day and night?
The command “be strong and courageous,” with the verb אָמַץ (’amats, “be firm, take heart”), is repeated four times: why do Joshua and the people need to hear it so many times?
“The LORD your God is with you wherever you go”: where are you going now that you need this assurance?
How does Rahab protect the spies and throw off the king of Jericho's men?
What does Rahab know about the God of Israel, and how did she come to know it?
Rahab asks the spies to treat her family with the same חֵסֵד (chesed, “kindness, loyalty”) she showed them: what does this word indicate about the agreement between them?
How is Rahab remembered in Matthew 1:5, Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25, and what does this say about who can enter God's people?
The scarlet cord in the window was a sign of protection: what signs of faith and hope do you keep visible in your life?
What distance were the people to keep from the ark, and for what reason?
Why does the crossing of the Jordan serve to show that God would be with Joshua as He was with Moses?
The text calls the אָרוֹן (’aron, “ark”) the ark “of the Lord of all the earth”: what does this title affirm before the peoples of Canaan?
The waters stopped only when the priests' feet touched the edge of the river: in what situation do you need to take the first step before seeing the way open?
What is done with the twelve stones taken from the Jordan, and where are the two sets of stones placed?
What link does the text make between the crossing of the Jordan and that of the Red Sea, and what is the purpose stated in v. 24?
Why does God command simple אֶבֶן (’even, “stones”) taken from the riverbed to be set up as a memorial, and not an elaborate monument?
“What do these stones mean to you?”: what “stones of remembrance” do you have to tell the young what God has done?
Why was it necessary to circumcise the Israelites at Gilgal?
What does the answer of the Commander of the LORD's army to Joshua's question change in the way of seeing the coming battle?
What does it mean that the new generation is marked by the verb מוּל (mul, “circumcise”) just before conquering the land?
The manna ceases when the people begin to eat the produce of the land: how do you recognize when God changes the way He cares for you?
What instructions does the LORD give for the first six days and for the seventh?
How can we read honestly the total destruction of Jericho alongside the rescue of Rahab and her family?
What role does the שׁוֹפָר (shofar, “ram's horn”) play in the taking of Jericho, and what does it recall in Israel's worship?
The people were to march in silence until the order to shout: at what moments is keeping silent and waiting harder for you than acting?
What happened in the first attack on Ai, and what advice had the spies given beforehand?
Why is the sin of one man treated as the sin of all “Israel”?
What did Achan take from the חֵרֶם (cherem, “devoted things”), and why was this so serious?
Achan says he saw, coveted, took and hid: at what point along this path do you usually notice the temptation?
What is Joshua's strategy for taking Ai on the second attempt?
What changes between the instructions about the plunder of Jericho and those for Ai?
Joshua writes the law on stones and reads it to everyone: why does the chapter insist on what was כָּתַב (katav, “written”) right after the victory?
The reading included women, children and foreigners: who is usually left out when the word of God is read and explained in your community?
What ruse do the Gibeonites use to seem to have come from a distant land?
How does the fate of the Gibeonites join curse and protection at the same time?
Why do the leaders keep what they had sworn, with the verb שָׁבַע (shava‘, “swear”), even after discovering the deception?
The Israelites examined the provisions and “did not seek the counsel of the LORD”: in what decisions do you usually trust only in what you see?
Why do the five Amorite kings attack Gibeon, and what do the Gibeonites ask of Joshua?
How do you understand the account of the sun and moon standing still, and what does v. 14 highlight as most extraordinary about that day?
The text repeats that the LORD לָחַם (lacham, “fought”) for Israel: how does this statement relate to the battles fought by the people themselves in the chapter?
“Do not be afraid or discouraged; be strong and courageous”: what past victory can give you courage for what you face now?
What forces do the northern kings gather, and what does Joshua do with the horses and chariots after the victory?
What does the text mean by attributing the hardening of the kings' hearts to the LORD, and how should this statement be read?
Why did Joshua שָׂרַף (saraf, “burn”) the chariots and only the city of Hazor, and not the other cities on their mounds?
Joshua did everything “leaving nothing undone” of what the LORD had commanded Moses: what guidance received from those who came before you in the faith have you sought to follow faithfully?
Which kings were defeated on the east side of the Jordan, still in the time of Moses?
Why does the book list the thirty-one kings one by one, instead of just giving the total?
The list repeats “one” (אֶחָד, ’echad) for each king defeated: what effect does this count have on those who read or hear the text?
The list begins with Moses' victories and continues with Joshua's: how do you recognize the work of those who came before in what you reap today?
What lands still remained to be possessed when Joshua was already old?
Why does the tribe of Levi receive no inheritance of land, and what, according to the text, is its inheritance?
Why does the text dwell so long on describing the גְּבוּל (gevul, “borders”) of each tribe?
Joshua is “old and advanced in years” and much land remains to be possessed: what is still left to do in your journey, whatever your age?
What does Caleb remind Joshua about the episode at Kadesh-barnea?
Why does Caleb ask precisely for the hill country where the Anakim and the great fortified cities were?
Caleb “followed the LORD wholeheartedly,” with the verb מָלֵא (male', “fill, complete”): what does this expression say about his faithfulness?
At eighty-five, Caleb still feels strong for the task: what challenge could you take on without thinking your time has passed?
How does Caleb take Hebron and Debir, and who receives Achsah as a wife?
Why does the text describe the borders of Judah in such detail, including the stretch that passes by Jerusalem (v. 8)?
The verb יָרַשׁ (yarash) means “possess” and also “drive out”: what does Caleb achieve at Hebron (v. 14) and what does Judah fail to do in Jerusalem (v. 63)?
Achsah boldly asks “Give me a blessing”: what have you hesitated to ask of God or of those who can help you?
What tribes make up the sons of Joseph, and where does the border of their portion run?
Why do some cities of Ephraim lie within the inheritance of Manasseh, and what does this suggest about the relationship between the two tribes?
The name אֶפְרַיִם (’Efrayim) recalls the idea of “being fruitful” (Gen 41:52): what relationship does this name have with the inheritance the tribe received?
The Canaanites of Gezer were not driven out but became forced laborers: in what area of your life do you accept a comfortable coexistence with something that should be dealt with?
How do the daughters of Zelophehad receive their inheritance, according to the command given to Moses?
What do the sons of Joseph complain about, and how does Joshua respond to the complaint?
Why is the land distributed by גּוֹרָל (goral, “lot”), and not by each tribe's choice?
Joshua says “you will clear it” before the forest and the iron chariots: in what situation do you expect to receive ready-made what you could win with effort?
Where is the tabernacle set up, and what situation is still pending for seven tribes?
Why does Joshua call the tribes “slack,” if the land was already subdued before them?
Why is the land first surveyed, described and divided into seven חֵלֶק (cheleq, “portions”) before the casting of lots?
The men walked through and described the land before receiving it: what concrete preparation do you need to make to take possession of what God has already given you?
Why does the inheritance of Simeon lie within the portion of Judah?
What does v. 47 tell about the Danites, and what does this suggest about the inheritance they received?
The borders “reach” and “touch” one another, with the verb פָּגַע (paga‘, “touch, meet”): what does this image suggest about life together between the tribes?
Joshua receives his inheritance last, after all the tribes: what does this gesture say to you about leadership and service?
What must someone who flees to a city of refuge do on arriving at the city gate?
Why do the cities of refuge also apply to the foreigner who lives among the Israelites?
Death “unintentionally and without malice” is described with the word דַּעַת (da‘at, “knowledge, intent”): what importance does intention have for justice in this chapter?
God provides refuge for those who caused harm without meaning to: how do you treat someone who hurt you unintentionally?
How many cities do the Levites receive in all, and how are they distributed among the families of Kohath, Gershon and Merari?
How does the end of the chapter sum up the fulfillment of the promises, and how does this fit with the accounts of land not yet conquered?
Why are the cities of מִקְלָט (miqlat, “refuge”) precisely among the cities given to the Levites?
“Not one of all the LORD's good promises failed”: what promise of God have you already seen fulfilled in your life?
What do the Reubenites, the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh do by the Jordan, and how do the other tribes react?
What reason do the eastern tribes give for the altar, and why do they call it a “witness”?
The same מִזְבֵּחַ (mizbeach, “altar”) is seen as rebellion and as a witness: what changes the way it is read?
Before going to war, Israel sends a delegation to talk: how do you usually act when you think someone has wronged you?
What does Joshua ask of the people regarding the Book of the Law and the gods of the nations?
What danger does Joshua see in mixing with the nations that remain, and what images does he use to describe it?
The chapter contrasts holding fast to the LORD and holding fast to the nations, with the verb דָּבַק (davaq, “cling, hold fast”): what does this verb suggest about the nature of faithfulness?
Joshua, near death, asks them to acknowledge that no good word has failed: what would you like to leave said to those who come after you?
What stages of Israel's history does Joshua recall, from Terah to the entry into Canaan?
Why does Joshua say “You are not able to serve the LORD” right after the people promise to serve Him?
The verb עָבַד (‘avad, “serve”) is repeated many times in the chapter: what kinds of service are at stake, and what distinguishes serving the LORD?
“Choose this day whom you will serve”: what choice do you need to renew today, and what does it mean for your household?
